extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; citizens and readers interested in constitutional structure, judiciary design, and federal government theory
extracted.subtask_description: Normative/prescriptive guidance and arguments about how to structure and distribute judicial power under a national constitution, including the scope of federal jurisdiction, the roles of supreme and inferior courts, and the relation between federal and state courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: National judiciary for inter-state disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The national judiciary ought to preside in all cases in which one State or its citizens are opposed to another State or its citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This secures equality of privileges and immunities across the Union and prevents local bias; federal tribunals, having no local attachments and owing their existence to the Union, are most likely to be impartial between different States and their citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit construction of fundamental provisions to impartial tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of fundamental constitutional provisions should be committed to a tribunal 'having no local attachments' and likely to be impartial between the States and their citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure full effect of key provisions and guard against evasion or subterfuge, interpretation should rest with a national court not subject to local prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: cases arising under Constitution and federal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend jurisdiction 'to all cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution and the laws of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes controversies that directly implicate constitutional prohibitions or federal statutes (example: emission of paper money contrary to constitutional prohibition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include equitable jurisdiction where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judiciary should have equitable as well as legal jurisdiction for causes involving fraud, accident, trust, or hardship arising under the Constitution and federal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity is necessary to relieve 'hard bargains' and other situations where legal remedies are inadequate; agreements concerning land under conflicting grants are cited as examples necessitating equitable jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction over treaties and diplomatic cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend jurisdiction 'to treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, and to all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These matters relate to preservation of national peace and foreign relations and therefore belong to national courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiralty and maritime jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts should have cognizance of admiralty and maritime causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maritime causes commonly depend on laws of nations and affect rights of foreigners, falling within considerations relative to public peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction where the United States is a party
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal judiciary to hear 'controversies to which the United States shall be a party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cases naturally belong to national tribunals because the federal government is itself involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction over controversies between States and various citizen permutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend jurisdiction 'to controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; between citizens of different States; between citizens of the same State claiming lands under grants of different States; and between a State or the citizens thereof and foreign states, citizens, and subjects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerated list constitutes the mass of judicial authority of the Union and is designed to address matters liable to local bias or implicating multiple sovereignties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court original jurisdiction narrow and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is confined to 'cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls, and those in which a State shall be a party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All other federal causes receive original cognizance in inferior tribunals; the Supreme Court's primary role is appellate, not initial trial, except for these rare classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court should be a distinct, independent body
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court ought to be a separate and independent body rather than a branch of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separateness prevents the same body that makes bad laws from being the final interpreter of them; legislative bodies lack the qualifications and independence appropriate for final judicial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial tenure during good behaviour and qualification by legal knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure of good behavior for judicial offices is recommended instead of temporary appointments; judges should be chosen for legal knowledge acquired by long and laborious study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent tenure insulates judges from partisan pressures and promotes consistent, informed adjudication; legislative members are unlikely to possess comparable qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislatures cannot reverse judicial sentences in particular cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature cannot, without exceeding its province, reverse a judicial determination once made in a particular case; it may prescribe new rules for future cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle applies equally to State and national governments and is a check on legislative encroachment into judicial determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to constitute inferior federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should have power to constitute inferior courts to obviate the necessity of recourse to the Supreme Court in every federal case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferior courts enable decentralized administration of federal justice, allow for circuit riding with state judges, and permit appeals to be circumscribed to a manageable compass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferior federal courts preferred to exclusive reliance on State courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on State courts for federal causes because local spirit and the tenure/independence of state judges may disqualify them for national jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State judges holding office during pleasure or short terms may be insufficiently independent; where state tribunals are trusted, Congress could commit jurisdiction, but explicit federal inferior courts should exist by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact, subject to exceptions by Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court shall possess appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact, and this jurisdiction shall be subject to such exceptions and regulations as Congress shall make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general grant allows the government to regulate appeals (including whether facts re-examined), avoids technically limiting appellate review based on any single State's procedures, and permits the use of remand, second juries, or issues directed out of the Supreme Court when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review does not abolish trial by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court does not necessarily imply the abolition of trial by jury; appeals may be regulated so as to preserve jury trials where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-examination of facts decided by a jury could be conducted via remand for a second jury or by directing an issue out of the Supreme Court; Congress may provide that appeals to the Supreme Court do not re-examine facts tried by juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts retain pre-existing jurisdiction; concurrent jurisdiction presumed
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts will retain the jurisdiction they now have unless it is expressly taken away by the Constitution or national legislation; concurrent jurisdiction in federal causes is the natural construction unless explicitly excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appeal should lie from State tribunals to the Supreme Court; holding the systems as 'one whole' supports using state courts as auxiliaries to execute laws of the Union while preserving avenues for national appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign immunity of States absent express consent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inherent in sovereignty not to be amenable to suit of an individual without its consent; States are not subject to suits by individuals unless they surrender that immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts with a sovereign bind conscience rather than compulsion; authorizing suits against States would be inconsistent with sovereignty unless explicitly provided for.
